title: Modesty brings good
hook: a man scolds his brother for being too shy, and the Prophet steps in

segments.voice: Yesterday, generosity that draws near, and your line: near through giving. Did one gift go out uncounted? Today, a quieter virtue, one that holds back instead. Day one thousand three hundred eight.

A man of the Ansar is lecturing his brother: you're too shy. You hold back too much. It's costing you. It's the kind of advice people still give. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, was passing by and heard it. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase, he said: leave him. Haya' is part of faith. He didn't side with the confident brother. He defended the shy one. Today's word: haya', and a short hadith that says it brings nothing but good.
screen: `YOU'RE TOO SHY.` → `LEAVE HIM.` → `HAYA' IS PART OF FAITH.`

segments.voice: Haya' is hard to put into one English word. Modesty, shyness, a sense of shame in the good sense, the inner brake that stops a hand before it does something low. The hadith of the day is from 'Imran ibn Husayn, in Bukhari, in paraphrase: haya' brings nothing but good. Not mostly good. Only good. So what is it, if it's always good? It isn't timidity, the fear that keeps someone from speaking a truth. It's closer to conscience with a blush. Abu Sa'id describes the Prophet himself, in Bukhari, in paraphrase: he was more shy than a young girl behind her curtain, and when he disliked something, you could see it in his face. A leader of a whole community, and his displeasure showed in his face. Then Bukhari keeps a saying the Prophet traced to the words of the first prophecy, in paraphrase: if you have no haya', do whatever you like. It reads like permission, but it's a warning. Without that inner brake, nothing stops anything. Haya' is what makes a person pause before the cruel comment, the post that shows off, the glance that takes too much. Tradition speaks of it facing two ways: haya' before people, and haya' before Allah, the sense of being seen even when the room is empty. Both work the same way. They make a person a little slower to do what they'd regret. That's why it brings only good.
screen: `MODESTY, SHYNESS, AN INNER BRAKE.` · `ONLY GOOD, NOT MOSTLY GOOD.` · `NO HAYA'? DO WHAT YOU LIKE.` · `BEFORE PEOPLE, BEFORE ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Let your shoulders drop. Run back through yesterday and look for a moment where a small pause might have helped: a joke that went one step too far, a story told mostly to look good, something shared that didn't need sharing. Don't judge it. Just find the spot where the brake could have touched. Now look ahead at today. Pick one place to let haya' work: speak a little less about yourself, dress or post with a little more restraint, or let someone else's mistake go unmentioned. If you pray, you can ask for haya'. The bell holds the time.
Haya'. Modesty and shyness, an inner brake before people and before Allah, that the hadith says brings nothing but good. Today's word.
Your line: only good. Today, let one pause happen before a word or a post, and see what it saves. Tomorrow, truthfulness and its company. Day one thousand three hundred eight.

howItsDone: In Islamic teaching, haya', modesty and shyness before people and before Allah, is part of faith, drawing on hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari that say haya' brings nothing but good.

original.note: Arabic: modesty, shyness, an inner brake.

trapdoor: what you thought: modesty is about clothes.
what it means: an inner brake before people and before Allah, in speech, glance and dress, that brings only good.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 24 and 6117, and the saying from 'the first prophecy' (Bukhari 3483); tradition speaks of haya' before people and haya' before Allah.

notes: Bukhari 24 says 'a man of the Ansar admonishing his brother'; the hook says 'a man is lecturing his brother' (the hadith may mean a brother in faith); confirm.
